doc.title: Reggie Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 22, 2018

title: College mentor Kevin Friesen and leaving for cruise ships
summary: Watkins describes bassist Kevin Friesen's intense rehearsals and open-minded influence, before he left for cruise ships.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: That’s terrific. Most musicians it seems have a moment that they figure I have to go to New York. Was that true for you?

Yeah it is in a way, it is in a way you know, but you know my first goal was the make a living playing music. And so I got out of college. Well first of all I was in college I had a great mentor, a relatively unknown bassist and composer, Kevin Friesen.

Friesen. Like David Friesen. No relation, but Kevin Friesen. And we were kind of in his camp. And he was serious, meaning a 10 p.m. to 8 a.m. rehearsal was not uncommon for us. So ninety percent of people that came through the door in his scene left immediately because he was too rough around the edges and it was too much of a commitment just work-wise and emotionally for a lot of people. But so I stayed. I was drawn to him and he was of course, he opened my mind up to everything: avante garde, he had thousands of records, incredibly versatile on electric and upright bass. So that was a real education. And I left there to go work on cruise ships. Then I went to Pittsburgh. I grew tired of the ships. Inside of two years I was done. So I made a little money, I got out, learned a lot of standards during that time, which was good.
